article.title: Jellyfin Loses Its Project Leader and Two Founding Contributors Within Days as Burnout and an AI-Tooling Dispute Surface
article.summary: Joshua Boniface, Anthony Lavado, and Andrew Rabert all left the open-source Jellyfin project within days, citing burnout and friction over AI-assisted development tools.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

Jellyfin, the open-source self-hosted media server, has lost three of its longest-standing contributors within a matter of days. Project leader Joshua Boniface and core team member Anthony Lavado announced on the [Jellyfin community forum](https://forum.jellyfin.org/t-project-leadership-changes) that they are departing effective July 19, 2026, a move that comes just two days after original project figure Andrew Rabert resigned from the organization on July 17, according to [Linuxiac](https://linuxiac.com/jellyfin-loses-project-leader-and-core-team-member-in-major-shake-up/).

## What We Know

Boniface, who has led Jellyfin since it launched in late 2018 as an open-source fork of Emby, cited burnout as his reason for stepping down. In his own words on the [forum announcement](https://forum.jellyfin.org/t-project-leadership-changes), he wrote: "I simply could no longer provide the effort (mental or time-wise) that the role demanded, and thus I was not performing my duties to an acceptable degree, facing severe burnout, and risks to my mental health. It was time to step aside."

He framed the transition as orderly, adding that "hand-off is ongoing and is amicable, and there is good communication lines, so there is little to no risk of a hostile fork or anything of that nature." Looking back at the project's growth, Boniface said he originally expected Jellyfin to be used by "a few hundred, or maybe if we were lucky, a few thousand" people; instead, as he put it, "it's the #1 FLOSS media server, a truly viable alternative to Plex for literally millions of server administrators and probably 10x that many individual users."

Lavado, who managed app-store operations, releases, and administrative work rather than active coding, said his departure stemmed from different circumstances after nearly eight years with the project. "After 7.5 - nearly 8 - years, it's been a long time since I've been able to give much of my free time to Jellyfin. My life is changing and I've got other things that must take priority," he wrote, while committing to help with the transition "even if it takes a year," according to [Linuxiac](https://linuxiac.com/jellyfin-loses-project-leader-and-core-team-member-in-major-shake-up/).

Rabert's exit followed a different path. In a [GitHub issue](https://github.com/andrewrabert/jellium-desktop/issues/609) announcing that his in-progress rewrite of Jellyfin's desktop client would be renamed and detached from the official project, Rabert explained that he had started the rewrite in December 2025 to fix long-standing problems with the previous desktop app, including HDR support and maintenance burdens tied to the Qt framework. "There were only a handful of organization members in support of how I was developing this - including part of the leadership team. However, the general attitude was very negative and increasingly burdensome and restrictive," he wrote, adding that "it eventually reached a point where I lost almost all motivation to dedicate my time to this." He said he "made the decision to leave the Jellyfin organization entirely on 2026-07-17 and continue development externally."

Rabert pointed to a specific flashpoint as "an early sign" of the friction: a [GitHub issue](https://github.com/andrewrabert/jellium-desktop/issues/109) filed against his repository in April 2026 titled "Inclusion of CLAUDE.md violates Jellyfin LLM policy against inclusion of LLM metafiles," arguing that a file associated with AI-assisted development tooling breached Jellyfin's rules against including such files in the codebase. Rabert closed that issue himself without acting on it, marking it "not planned." Linuxiac reported that Rabert "cited increasing disagreements over the development approach, including opposition to his use of AI-assisted tools," and that his desktop-client project has since been renamed Jellium Desktop.

The dispute lands against a backdrop the project itself had already flagged. In its own ["State of the Fin" update published in May](https://jellyfin.org/posts/state-of-the-fin-2026-05-24/), the Jellyfin team wrote that it had been "inundated with AI-authored pull requests of varying quality," prompting it to create a formal LLM/AI policy, and acknowledged that "the increased support requests, combined with the AI code submissions, have led to burnout at various levels of the development and admin team." That same post credited Rabert by name as the developer leading the desktop client's shift away from Qt toward Chromium Embedded Framework and a modern mpv-based playback pipeline.

## What We Don't Know

Jellyfin has not detailed a formal succession plan for who will take over Boniface's and Lavado's responsibilities, and Linuxiac noted that the close timing of all three departures "raises questions about Jellyfin's governance and who will take responsibility for the many duties previously handled by its longtime leaders." It is also not yet clear whether Jellyfin's official desktop client will be rebuilt through a different path now that Rabert's rewrite has moved outside the organization, or whether any of the team's broader AI-tooling rules will be revisited as a result of the dispute.

## Analysis

The episode illustrates a structural tension increasingly visible across volunteer-run open-source projects: the same growth that validates a project's usefulness, Jellyfin's expansion from a niche Emby fork to what Boniface called the "#1 FLOSS media server", also multiplies the unpaid labor of support, review, and moderation that falls on a small core team. Layered on top of that is a newer strain specific to this moment in software development: maintainers setting boundaries around AI-assisted contributions while at least some contributors push back against those boundaries. Both Boniface's and Rabert's departures describe the same underlying pressure, an unsustainable volume of demands on volunteer time, even though they trace to different immediate causes.
